newsitem.title: UK: Clinton aide wants to help Britain's Labour - paper.
newsitem.headline: Clinton aide wants to help Britain's Labour - paper.

text.p: White House aide George Stephanopoulos, fresh from helping President Bill Clinton to his second election win, now wants to work for Britain's opposition Labour party, the Guardian newspaper said on Thursday.
"I've told them I'm happy to help if they want me," he told the newspaper, hours after hearing Clinton had won a second four-year term.

Stephanopoulos said he had not come to any formal agreement with Labour, which is trying to end 17 straight years of Conservative rule, but would try to do for party leader Tony Blair what he had done for Clinton.

"I know how to work the last 90 days of a campaign...how to respond to the tried-and-true techniques of the right wing," said the 35-year-old aide, who has made no secret of his desire to leave the Clinton administration.

He said he would not be involved in hands-on campaigning for Labour but would provide advice "to help translate the lessons of Bill Clinton" for Britain before the next general election, which must be held by next May.
"We know him and rate him highly. We would welcome any input he could feasibly make," the paper quoted Blair's office as saying.
If Stephanopoulos did work for Labour it would further chill the already cool relations between British Prime Minister John Major and the Clinton administration.

Although leaders of both countries insist their relations are as close as ever, insiders say the White House has never forgiven the Conservatives for aiding former president George Bush when he ran against Clinton in the 1992 election.

Blair and Clinton share the same political outlook as well as personal interests and held cordial White House talks in April which confirmed the impression given by America's elite that they saw him as a British prime minister-in-waiting.
Senior Blair aide Peter Mandelson was watching in the wings with Stephanopoulos last month when Clinton and Republican challenger Bob Dole held the second of their two televised pre-election debates.

"I realised he was not only a first-rate campaigner, but serious and committed in his politics, someone who could have a lot of sympathy with the economic and social policies Labour stands for," Mandelson told the Guardian.
